subject: english-language

moments.title: Caxton sets up shop at Westminster
moments.body: Caxton, who had learned printing in Cologne and Bruges, sets up England's first printing press at Westminster. He prints around 100 books, mostly in English — Chaucer, Malory's Le Morte d'Arthur, his own translations. He faces a dialectal decision: which English to use?

quote.text: Loo, what sholde a man in thyse days now wryte, egges or eyren?

moments.takeaway: Caxton tells a story of merchants who couldn't get eggs because the locals didn't recognise the word. He chose East Midlands English (the dialect of London and the university towns) — the basis of modern Standard English.

moments.title: King James Bible
moments.body: The KJV becomes the most influential book in English. Its rhythms, its archaisms (already slightly old-fashioned in 1611), its absorption into common speech — 'the salt of the earth', 'a thorn in the flesh', 'the writing on the wall', 'the powers that be' — shape literary English for four centuries.
moments.takeaway: Together with Shakespeare's First Folio (1623), the KJV gives early modern English a prestigious standard.

moments.title: Johnson's Dictionary
moments.body: Johnson's 'A Dictionary of the English Language' — 42,773 entries, written largely by Johnson alone over nine years — is the most influential dictionary before the OED. It uses illustrative quotations from literature, sets a tone of judicious authority, and helped fix spelling and meaning for the next century.
moments.takeaway: Johnson initially intended to 'fix' the language but came to accept that change was inevitable. The Preface is one of the great essays on lexicography.

now.title: Standard English now
now.body: Standard British English (sometimes 'BBC English' or 'received standard') is a written norm with broad consensus and a much looser spoken norm. American English diverged enough by the 19th century — Webster's 1828 dictionary deliberately reforms spelling (color, theater) and codifies an American standard. Global Englishes (Indian, Nigerian, Singaporean) are now spoken by more people than British and American combined.
now.open_questions: Will English fragment into mutually unintelligible varieties as Latin did into the Romance languages? Probably not, given continuous global media contact — but the question is taken seriously by linguists like David Crystal.

reflection: Standard English wasn't decreed; it was selected — by a printer's economic choice, a king's commission, a lexicographer's stamina, and a market of readers.
